title: Large dot products cause vanishing gradients in softmax for high dimensions
description: For large values of d_k, dot products grow large in magnitude, pushing the softmax function into regions where it has extremely small gradients, motivating the scaling factor 1/√d_k.
canonical_description: large-magnitude dot products cause vanishing gradients in softmax for high-dimensional keys and queries

verdict.reasoning: Two papers (periodic softmax alternatives and SA-Softmax) address the broader problem of softmax gradient vanishing from extreme inputs, but neither isolates or solves the specific gap: that dot products grow as √d_k in high dimensions, motivating the 1/√d_k scaling factor. Paper 1 does not analyze the dimension-scaling problem, compare against 1/√d_k, or test on standard transformer architectures; it also notes a separate issue ("oblivion of the most contributing value") as dimension increases. Paper 2 modifies softmax to x·softmax(x) to improve gradient flow, but does not study whether or how this relates to d_k scaling. Papers 3 and 4 investigate different phenomena (sample complexity of sigmoid vs. softmax attention, and over-centralization of softmax with many slots) and are irrelevant to the gap. No paper directly analyzes the √d_k growth problem, proposes an improvement to the 1/√d_k scaling factor, or demonstrates a solution that specifically addresses high-dimensional keys and queries causing vanishing softmax gradients.

paper.title: Escaping the Gradient Vanishing: Periodic Alternatives of Softmax in Attention Mechanism
paper.abstract: Softmax is widely used in neural networks for multiclass classification, gate structure and attention mechanisms. The statistical assumption that the input is normal distributed supports the gradient stability of Softmax. However, when used in attention mechanisms such as transformers, since the correlation scores between embeddings are often not normally distributed, the gradient vanishing problem appears, and we prove this point through experimental confirmation. In this work, we suggest that replacing the exponential function by periodic functions, and we delve into some potential periodic alternatives of Softmax from the view of value and gradient. Through experiments on a simply designed demo referenced to LeViT, our method is proved to be able to alleviate the gradient problem and yield substantial improvements compared to Softmax and its variants. Further, we analyze the impact of pre-normalization for Softmax and our methods through mathematics and experiments. Lastly, we increase the depth of the demo and prove the applicability of our method in deep structures.

assessments.contribution_summary: This paper identifies that softmax in attention mechanisms suffers from gradient vanishing when input values (Q·K) are large, and proposes replacing the exponential function with periodic functions (Sin-Softmax, Sin2-max-shifted, etc.) to compress inputs into non-saturating regions. The paper provides mathematical analysis of gradient properties, demonstrates that the input distribution is not strictly normal (contrary to the assumption that justifies 1/√d_k scaling), and shows experimentally that their periodic alternatives alleviate the gradient problem and improve performance on a LeViT-like demo.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper addresses a broader gradient vanishing problem in softmax attention (caused by non-normally-distributed inputs), but does not specifically isolate or solve the problem of large dot products scaling with dimension d_k. The canonical gap is about the specific scaling issue where dot products grow as √d_k, motivating the 1/√d_k factor. The paper's periodic alternatives (e.g., Sin-Softmax compressing via sin(x) ∈ [-1,1]) would indeed prevent large-magnitude inputs regardless of dimension, but the paper does not analyze the dimension-scaling problem explicitly, does not compare against the standard 1/√d_k scaling solution, and does not test on standard transformer architectures (only a small LeViT-like demo). The paper also acknowledges that periodic alternatives may cause "oblivion of the most contributing value" as dimension increases, which is a separate issue not addressed.

paper.title: Self-Adjust Softmax
paper.abstract: The softmax function is crucial in Transformer attention, which normalizes each row of the attention scores with summation to one, achieving superior performances over other alternative functions. However, the softmax function can face a gradient vanishing issue when some elements of the attention scores approach extreme values, such as probabilities close to one or zero. In this paper, we propose Self-Adjust Softmax (SA-Softmax) to address this issue by modifying $softmax(x)$ to $x \cdot softmax(x)$ and its normalized variant $\frac{(x - min(x_{\min},0))}{max(0,x_{max})-min(x_{min},0)} \cdot softmax(x)$. We theoretically show that SA-Softmax provides enhanced gradient properties compared to the vanilla softmax function. Moreover, SA-Softmax Attention can be seamlessly integrated into existing Transformer models to their attention mechanisms with minor adjustments. We conducted experiments to evaluate the empirical performance of Transformer models using SA-Softmax compared to the vanilla softmax function. These experiments, involving models with up to 2.7 billion parameters, are conducted across diverse datasets, language tasks, and positional encoding methods.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper proposes Self-Adjust Softmax (SA-Softmax), which modifies the standard softmax function to x·softmax(x) and its normalized variants, to mitigate the gradient vanishing problem that occurs when softmax inputs become extreme (very large or small). This directly addresses the same underlying issue described in the gap — large dot products causing vanishing gradients in softmax — but proposes a different solution (modifying the softmax function itself) rather than analyzing or improving the scaling factor 1/√d_k. The paper provides theoretical gradient analysis showing improved gradient propagation and conducts extensive experiments demonstrating performance improvements across various model sizes, position encodings, and downstream tasks.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper does not specifically address the high-dimensional scaling problem (large d_k) that motivates the 1/√d_k factor. It does not analyze whether its method works specifically when d_k is large, nor does it compare against or improve upon the standard 1/√d_k scaling. The paper's solution is an alternative modification to softmax rather than a direct solution to the problem of large dot products in high dimensions. The gap about understanding/improving the scaling factor 1/√d_k for high-dimensional keys and queries remains open.
evidence_snippets: One of the primary limitations of softmax lies in its susceptibility to the gradient vanishing problem. When input values to the softmax function become highly polarized, i.e., extreme values that are very large or small, the resulting probabilities can exhibit extreme sparsity. This, in turn, leads to gradients that approach zero, impeding effective learning and optimization during backpropagation.

To address this issue, we propose modifying the attention mechanism by scaling the softmax output with its input, called \methodFullName (\methodShortName). Specifically, we redefine the output of attention scores as follows: β_{i,j} = z_{i,j} · softmax(z_{i,j})

In the standard softmax attention, the gradient softmax output α_{i,j} with respect to the input z_{i,j} tends to vanish when α_{i,j} approaches 0 or 1. By introducing an additional self-adjusting term in the attention score computation (i.e., modufying softmax(x) to x · softmax(x)), we allow for a more resilient gradient.

paper.title: Sigmoid Self-Attention has Lower Sample Complexity than Softmax Self-Attention: A Mixture-of-Experts Perspective
paper.abstract: At the core of the popular Transformer architecture is the self-attention mechanism, which dynamically assigns softmax weights to each input token so that the model can focus on the most salient information. However, the softmax structure slows down the attention computation due to its row-wise nature, and it inherently introduces competition among tokens: as the weight assigned to one token increases, the weights of others decrease. This competitive dynamic may narrow the focus of self-attention to a limited set of features, potentially overlooking other informative characteristics. Recent experimental studies have shown that using the element-wise sigmoid function helps eliminate token competition and reduce the computational overhead. Despite these promising empirical results, a rigorous comparison between sigmoid and softmax self-attention mechanisms remains absent in the literature. This paper closes this gap by theoretically demonstrating that sigmoid self-attention is more sample-efficient than its softmax counterpart. Toward that goal, we represent the self-attention matrix as a mixture of experts and show that ``experts'' in sigmoid self-attention require significantly less data to achieve the same approximation error as those in softmax self-attention.

assessments.contribution_summary: This paper theoretically compares the sample complexity of sigmoid self-attention versus softmax self-attention by connecting both to Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models. It shows that under the "dense regime" (which is more common in practice), sigmoid self-attention requires only O(ε^{-2}) data points to achieve approximation error ε, while softmax self-attention requires O(ε^{-4}) or even O(exp(ε^{-1/τ})) data points. The paper does not address the problem of large dot products causing vanishing gradients in softmax.
assessments.what_remains_open: The entire gap remains open. The paper does not discuss, analyze, or propose any solution to the problem of large dot products causing vanishing gradients in the softmax function for high-dimensional keys and queries. It does not address the scaling factor 1/√d_k, gradient magnitudes, or the saturation behavior of softmax in high dimensions. The paper focuses on a completely different issue: comparing sample complexity (data efficiency) between sigmoid and softmax attention mechanisms.

paper.title: A Study on ReLU and Softmax in Transformer
paper.abstract: The Transformer architecture consists of self-attention and feed-forward networks (FFNs) which can be viewed as key-value memories according to previous works. However, FFN and traditional memory utilize different activation functions (i.e., ReLU and Softmax respectively), which makes them not equivalent. In this paper, we first rebuild the connections between FFN and key-value memory by conducting extensive studies on ReLU and Softmax, and find they are equivalent when adding an additional layer normalization module on Softmax. In addition, ReLU outperforms Softmax on both FFN and key-value memory when the number of value slots is large. We analyze the reasons and then explore this good property of ReLU on the self-attention network where the original Softmax activation performs poorly on long input sequences. We then propose a full ReLU architecture named ReLUFormer which performs better than the baseline Transformer on long sequence tasks such as document translation. This paper sheds light on the following points: 1) Softmax and ReLU use different normalization methods over elements which lead to different variances of results, and ReLU is good at dealing with a large number of key-value slots; 2) FFN and key-value memory are equivalent, and thus the Transformer can be viewed as a memory network where FFNs and self-attention networks are both key-value memories.

assessments.contribution_summary: This paper studies the differences between ReLU and Softmax activation functions in Transformer architectures (FFN and self-attention). It finds that Softmax produces over-centralized distributions that fail to utilize many value slots when the number of slots is large, while ReLU can better handle large numbers of slots. The paper proposes a full ReLU architecture (ReLUFormer) with variance reduction and regularization techniques to make ReLU work in self-attention, showing improvements on long document translation. However, the paper does not address the problem of large dot products causing vanishing gradients in softmax for high-dimensional keys and queries.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper does not address the specific gap: that large dot products (from high-dimensional keys/queries) push softmax into regions with extremely small gradients, which motivates the scaling factor 1/√d_k. The paper focuses on a different issue — Softmax's over-centralization when there are many slots — and proposes replacing Softmax with ReLU as an alternative. The original problem of vanishing gradients in softmax due to large-magnitude dot products in high dimensions remains entirely unaddressed. The paper does not analyze, measure, or propose any solution for the vanishing gradient phenomenon in softmax.

ranking.feasibility_reasoning: The gap is well-scoped and evaluable: compare any proposed alternative to the standard 1/√d_k scaling on gradient magnitude, convergence speed, and downstream task performance. Data and compute requirements are modest — the problem can be studied analytically (mathematical analysis of softmax gradient properties under different scalings) or with small transformer training runs on standard benchmarks (Wikitext, GLUE, etc.), not frontier-scale compute. Prior work (periodic softmax, SA-Softmax) provides methodological starting points. The main challenge is that 1/√d_k is already a simple, well-understood, and effective fix; finding a *meaningfully better* alternative that generalizes across architectures and tasks may be difficult, and some attempted solutions could yield negative results. This makes the gap tractable (focused, measurable, low resource barrier) but not trivial — the risk is incremental or null progress rather than infeasibility.
